attributes.Description:
The church at Astwick stands in the midst of a cluster of farm buildings with some evidence of earthworks in the surrounding area. This also includes the mill stream and a hollow way leading north to south. At the centre of the complex is Astwick Bury moated manor house complex. [1] Astwick was mentioned in Domesday, but appears to have always been small. The Domesday reference includes two mills. [2] It has a church with a record in the 1291 Taxatio. It continues through much of the documentary evidence with a 1334 Lay Subsidy but in most it is included with other settlements. In essence this is a shrunken settlement as it was probably not much bigger than currently survives.

Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

attributes.Description:
The settlement of Cainhoe is thought to be located somewhere between the remains of the motte and bailey castle at Cainhoe to the north and Cainhoe Manor to the south. The grid reference has been altered from the original (TL 100 367) to reflect this location more closely. Earthworks close to the castle that were originally thought to have been part of the settlement are now thought to be a continuation of the castle features. [1] A hollow way has been spotted on the earlier aerial photographs but this area has been heavily quarried. [1]

Cainhoe was recorded in Domesday with a minimum population of 15 and later in the 1334 Lay Subsidy the village was taxed alongside the village of Clophill. There is also an E179 date of 1624 for the settlement. The site was held by the d'Albini family following the conquest, and it is suggested that the village was deserted soon after 1349 as a consequence of the Black Death. [1] An inquisition post mortem of 1375 found ten cottages that were empty ‘since the pestilence’. [2]

Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

attributes.Description:
Traces of the village earthworks are visible to the north and the west of St Nicholas’s Church. [1] The principal remains are a hollow way which bisects the site running east to west, bounded by a moat to the east and two building platforms to the west. Other surrounding features include further building platforms to the south of the hollow way and a possible moat or fish pond. [1, 2] A large moated site is present to the northeast of the church and to the north of the present hall which was built in 1847. [3]

Landwade is first mentioned in 1060 however there is no mention of the settlement in the Domesday Book. [4] In 1279, it is recorded with 12 households not including the Manor House. [1] By 1327, this number had increased to 15 households. In 1334, the tax quota was well below the national average at 40s. [5] There was a boom during the later fourteenth century when the village went through a revival and the 1377 records showed 44 tax payers. [4] However by 1664 only 8 households remained in the village and by 1674, there were only 4 [1]. It would appear that the village had begun its decline around 1563. [4]

Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

attributes.Description:
Only faint traces are visible on aerial photographs and the area is now heavily ploughed. Located 5 km to the north of Burstwick it has been described as a hamlet. [1] Although mentioned in Domesday, as a berewick of Burstwick, there is little later evidence of the settlement. There are details of landownership and inheritances but substantial settlement is not indicated. Burstwick North Park may have taken part of the area of Nuthill in the twelfth century. [1, 2] The park was in place by 1260. [2] A moated manor house was mentioned in 1301, however there were no tenants. [1, 3, 4] A chapel was recorded from between 1154-1180 but issues with the vacant living are recorded from 1301 onwards, and the chapel was no longer standing by c. 1700. [1] Most of the land in the area was enclosed by the end of the sixteenth century. [1]

Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

attributes.Description:
The site can be seen on the ground as faint crop marks in an area of ploughing. An east-west hollow way is visible with possible field boundaries. However the HER suggests that these are not settlement remains but evidence of water meadows. [1] To the south-west there was once the earthwork remains of a defensive site which has now been badly damaged but may have also had associated settlement. [2] Part of the site has also been damaged by the straightening of the River Ivel. The documentary evidence for the site is confused. The manor of Etonbury seems to be combined with Arlesey which has extensive Domesday and later evidence. Etonbury itself does not appear in any taxation records and it may be the case that there was no extensive settlement at Etonbury, instead a manorial complex is present with the population located at Arlesey.

Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.
